title: Basic Nursing Care — Fluid & Electrolyte Basics and IV Observation (Set 12)
subtitle: Fluid balance and overload, daily weights and accurate I&O, at-risk clients, electrolyte function and imbalance warning signs, and observing an IV site safely within scope (recognizing problems, reporting, never adjusting the rate)
scenario: Helping keep clients in safe fluid and electrolyte balance: monitoring intake/output and weight, recognizing dehydration, fluid overload, and electrolyte-imbalance warning signs, and observing an IV site while leaving IV therapy to licensed staff.

steps.q: Why is fluid balance important to monitor?

opts.text: Both too little fluid (dehydration) and too much fluid (overload) can harm the body and must be recognized
opts.rat: The body works best in balance; monitoring catches both dehydration and fluid overload, each of which is dangerous.

opts.text: Only dehydration is ever a problem
opts.rat: Fluid overload is also harmful; both extremes matter.

opts.text: Only fluid overload is ever a problem
opts.rat: Dehydration is equally important to recognize.

opts.text: Fluid balance has no effect on health
opts.rat: Fluid balance is essential to circulation, organ function, and safety.

steps.q: Which findings suggest possible FLUID OVERLOAD?

opts.text: Swelling (edema), sudden weight gain, puffiness, and shortness of breath
opts.rat: Excess fluid collects in tissues and the lungs, producing edema, rapid weight gain, and breathing difficulty.

opts.text: Dry mouth, sunken eyes, and very dark urine
opts.rat: These point to dehydration, not overload.

opts.text: Strong thirst with poor skin turgor
opts.rat: Thirst and poor turgor suggest dehydration.

opts.text: Weight loss with concentrated urine
opts.rat: Weight loss and concentrated urine suggest fluid deficit, not overload.

steps.q: Daily weights are a valuable way to track fluid status because:

opts.text: A rapid change in weight often reflects a change in body fluid, so weights are taken consistently (same time, scale, and clothing)
opts.rat: Short-term weight changes largely reflect fluid gain or loss; consistent technique makes the trend reliable.

opts.text: Weight has nothing to do with fluid balance
opts.rat: Rapid weight changes are closely tied to fluid shifts.

opts.text: Weighing at random times gives the best data
opts.rat: Inconsistent timing/technique makes the trend unreliable.

opts.text: Only monthly weights matter for fluid status
opts.rat: Fluid changes can occur quickly, so daily weights are used when monitoring fluid status.

steps.q: When keeping intake and output (I&O) records, the technician should:

opts.text: Measure and record all intake and output accurately rather than estimating
opts.rat: Accurate measurement makes I&O useful for detecting fluid imbalance; guessing undermines its value.

opts.text: Estimate the amounts to save time
opts.rat: Estimating reduces accuracy and can mask a developing imbalance.

opts.text: Record only what the client drinks, never output
opts.rat: Both intake and output must be recorded for a complete picture.

opts.text: Record intake only at the end of the week
opts.rat: I&O is recorded in real time so trends are accurate and timely.

steps.q: Which client is at the GREATEST risk for a fluid or electrolyte imbalance?

opts.text: An older adult with vomiting and diarrhea who depends on others to bring fluids
opts.rat: Fluid losses from vomiting/diarrhea plus limited ability to obtain fluids and age-related factors greatly increase imbalance risk.

opts.text: A healthy adult drinking normally
opts.rat: Normal intake and no losses make imbalance unlikely.

opts.text: A client eating and drinking well with no losses
opts.rat: Good intake without losses is low risk.

opts.text: A client with stable weight and normal output
opts.rat: Stable weight and output suggest balance, not risk.

steps.q: A client has had several episodes of vomiting and diarrhea. The technician should recognize that this can cause loss of:

opts.text: Both fluids and electrolytes, so the client should be monitored and the losses reported
opts.rat: Vomiting and diarrhea remove water and electrolytes; monitoring and reporting allow timely correction and prevent complications.

opts.text: Nothing of importance to the body
opts.rat: These losses can quickly cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

opts.text: Only calories, not fluids
opts.rat: Significant fluid and electrolyte loss occurs, not just calories.

opts.text: Only fat stores
opts.rat: The concern is fluid and electrolyte loss, not fat.

steps.q: Electrolytes (such as sodium and potassium) are important because they:

opts.text: Help the heart, muscles, and nerves function properly
opts.rat: Electrolytes are essential minerals that support normal heart rhythm, muscle contraction, and nerve signaling.

opts.text: Have no role in body function
opts.rat: Electrolytes are vital to many body processes.

opts.text: Only affect the color of the skin
opts.rat: Their role is far broader—heart, muscle, and nerve function.

opts.text: Are only important during exercise
opts.rat: Electrolyte balance matters at all times, not only during exercise.

steps.q: Why is a significant potassium imbalance particularly concerning?

opts.text: It can affect the heart's rhythm, so related symptoms should be reported promptly
opts.rat: Potassium strongly influences cardiac rhythm; imbalances can cause dangerous arrhythmias, making prompt reporting important.

opts.text: It only changes the taste of food
opts.rat: Potassium's key concern is its effect on the heart and muscles, not taste.

opts.text: It has no effect on the body
opts.rat: Potassium is critical to heart and muscle function.

opts.text: It only matters in children
opts.rat: Potassium balance matters across all ages.

steps.q: Which findings could signal an electrolyte imbalance the technician should report?

opts.text: New muscle weakness or cramps, confusion, an irregular pulse, or a change in alertness
opts.rat: Electrolyte imbalances commonly affect muscles, nerves, and the heart, producing weakness/cramps, confusion, irregular pulse, or altered alertness.

opts.text: Normal strength, clear thinking, and a regular pulse
opts.rat: These are reassuring, normal findings.

opts.text: A calm client resting comfortably
opts.rat: This is not a warning sign.

opts.text: Steady mood and usual activity level
opts.rat: Baseline stability is not a concern to report.

steps.q: When the technician notices possible signs of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance, the appropriate action is to:

opts.text: Recognize the signs and report them to the nurse for evaluation
opts.rat: The technician observes and reports; evaluating and treating imbalances is done by licensed staff.

opts.text: Diagnose the specific imbalance and start treatment
opts.rat: Diagnosing and treating are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Give the client extra electrolyte pills independently
opts.rat: Administering supplements without an order is outside scope and unsafe.

opts.text: Ignore the signs unless the client complains loudly
opts.rat: Signs are reported when noticed, not only when the client complains.

steps.q: Regarding a client's IV (intravenous) therapy, the psychiatric technician's role is generally to:

opts.text: Observe the IV site and the client and report concerns—not to start the IV, regulate the rate, or give IV medications
opts.rat: Within scope, the technician monitors and reports; starting, adjusting, and medicating IVs are done by licensed staff.

opts.text: Independently start and program the IV pump
opts.rat: Starting and programming IV therapy is outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Adjust the IV flow rate as they see fit
opts.rat: Only licensed staff set/adjust the IV rate per order.

opts.text: Push medications into the IV line
opts.rat: Administering IV medications is outside the technician's scope.

steps.q: While observing an IV site, which finding should the technician report as a possible problem?

opts.text: Redness, swelling, warmth or coolness, pain, or fluid leaking around the site
opts.rat: These can indicate infiltration, phlebitis, or infection at the IV site and should be reported promptly.

opts.text: A clean, dry site with no redness or swelling
opts.rat: A normal-looking site is not a concern.

opts.text: The client resting comfortably with no complaints
opts.rat: No complaints and comfort are reassuring, not a problem.

opts.text: Intact, well-secured tubing
opts.rat: Properly secured tubing is expected, not a concern.

steps.q: A client says the IV site is burning and painful. The technician should:

opts.text: Notify the nurse promptly and not adjust the IV themselves
opts.rat: Pain/burning may signal a site problem; the technician reports it right away and leaves any IV adjustment to licensed staff.

opts.text: Speed up the IV to flush the discomfort away
opts.rat: Changing the IV rate is outside scope and could worsen harm.

opts.text: Ignore it since IVs are 'supposed to' hurt
opts.rat: Burning pain is not normal and should be reported.

opts.text: Remove the IV independently
opts.rat: Discontinuing an IV is done by licensed staff, not the technician, and it should first be reported.

steps.q: To help keep a client's IV functioning safely, the technician can:

opts.text: Keep the site dry, avoid kinks in the tubing, and prevent the client from pulling on the line
opts.rat: These simple protective measures help maintain the IV without adjusting the therapy itself.

opts.text: Let the tubing kink under the client's body
opts.rat: Kinked tubing interrupts flow and should be avoided.

opts.text: Encourage the client to tug on the line for comfort
opts.rat: Pulling on the line can dislodge the IV and cause injury.

opts.text: Soak the IV dressing during bathing
opts.rat: Keeping the site dry helps prevent infection and dressing failure.

steps.q: Which IV-related situation should the technician report to the nurse?

opts.text: The IV pump is alarming, the bag is empty, the drip has stopped, or the line has become disconnected
opts.rat: These indicate the IV needs attention from licensed staff and should be reported promptly.

opts.text: The IV is running as ordered with a comfortable client
opts.rat: Normal function with a comfortable client is not a concern.

opts.text: The dressing is clean, dry, and intact
opts.rat: An intact dressing is expected, not a problem.

opts.text: The client is resting quietly
opts.rat: Restful comfort is not a reportable IV problem.

steps.q: When helping a client with an IV move or transfer, the technician should:

opts.text: Protect the site and tubing so the IV is not pulled or dislodged
opts.rat: Supporting the arm and managing the tubing during movement prevents dislodging the IV and causing injury.

opts.text: Let the tubing catch on the bed rails during the transfer
opts.rat: Snagging the tubing can dislodge the IV; it should be managed carefully.

opts.text: Pull the client by the IV arm
opts.rat: Pulling on the IV arm risks dislodging the line and injuring the client.

opts.text: Disconnect the IV to make moving easier
opts.rat: Disconnecting the IV is outside scope and risks contamination and interruption of therapy.

steps.q: Regarding oral fluids, the technician should:

opts.text: Encourage or restrict fluids according to the client's care plan and orders
opts.rat: Some clients need encouragement to drink while others are on fluid restriction; the technician follows the individualized order.

opts.text: Always push maximum fluids on every client
opts.rat: Some clients are on fluid restriction; more is not always better.

opts.text: Always restrict fluids for every client
opts.rat: Many clients need adequate or increased intake; restriction is order-specific.

opts.text: Ignore the care plan and let the client decide entirely
opts.rat: Intake is guided by the care plan, especially when a restriction or goal exists.

steps.q: A client on daily weights has a notable weight gain since yesterday. The technician should:

opts.text: Report the change to the nurse, since a rapid gain may indicate fluid retention
opts.rat: A sudden weight increase can reflect fluid retention/overload and should be reported for evaluation.

opts.text: Assume the scale is wrong and ignore it
opts.rat: Rather than dismissing it, the technician verifies technique and reports the change.

opts.text: Restrict the client's food to reverse the gain
opts.rat: Restricting food is not the response; the change is reported for evaluation.

opts.text: Wait a week before mentioning it
opts.rat: A rapid change is reported promptly, not after a week.

steps.q: A client with dehydration signs who is allowed oral fluids would benefit MOST from the technician:

opts.text: Offering fluids frequently within the care plan and monitoring intake and output
opts.rat: Regularly offering permitted fluids and tracking I&O supports rehydration and detects whether balance is improving.

opts.text: Withholding fluids until the next meal
opts.rat: Withholding fluids worsens dehydration.

opts.text: Waiting for the client to ask before offering anything
opts.rat: At-risk clients may not ask; the technician offers fluids proactively within the plan.

opts.text: Giving only dry foods
opts.rat: Dry foods do not address the fluid deficit.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in fluid, electrolyte, and IV care is to:

opts.text: Monitor I&O and weights, recognize dehydration/overload/imbalance signs, observe the IV site, and report—leaving IV therapy management to licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician's contributions are monitoring, recognition, observation, and reporting; managing IV therapy is done by licensed staff.

opts.text: Independently manage all IV therapy and fluid orders
opts.rat: Managing IV therapy and writing fluid orders are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Diagnose and treat electrolyte imbalances
opts.rat: Diagnosis and treatment are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Ignore fluid status since it is not important
opts.rat: Fluid and electrolyte status is important and is actively monitored and reported.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (fluid and electrolyte basics and IV observation). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Fluid balance/overload signs, daily-weight and accurate-I&O monitoring, at-risk clients, the general role of electrolytes (heart/muscle/nerve function), potassium's effect on cardiac rhythm, and warning signs of imbalance are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation. Specific electrolyte reference values and IV flow rates/calculations are intentionally NOT asserted. IV content reflects the technician's scope: observe the site and client and report problems (redness/swelling/pain/leaking, pump alarms, empty bag, disconnection), while starting, regulating, medicating, or discontinuing IV therapy is performed by licensed staff. Builds on dehydration/I&O items in bnc-core-02/06 and fluid-encouragement/low-sodium items in bnc-core-05. Pending faculty review.
